articles.title: Socialism Wins in a Purple District
articles.author: Geovanny Tolentino and Jordan Millett
articles.content_excerpt: When State Representative Lesly Muñoz attended a Salem DSA meeting in October 2025, her district was under an ICE attack. Agents had kidnapped a father in the parking lot of El Torito Market. Days later, ICE abducted 31 immigrant workers in nearby Woodburn. Chapter leaders spent the better part of an hour brainstorming a rapid response with Lesly. By the end, we had a plan: activate community members by distributing Know Your Rights resources to residents and Latino businesses, with Lesly leveraging her position as state representative to amplify our Abolish ICE demands. That same evening, Lesly joined DSA. Together, we went on to build a campaign for the state legislature that mobilized constituents, named the enemy, and let the red banner fly. These ordinary differences can affect how each person experiences movement, pressure, and support throughout the night. articles.title: Statement from UAW President Shawn Fain and UAW Vice President Ryan Hiestand on Delphi Retirees
articles.author: Justin Mayhugh
articles.content_excerpt: The UAW is happy to announce that GM has agreed to honor its commitments to Delphi retirees who were denied annual lumpsum payments in 2023, 2024, 2025, and 2026. The remaining eligible Delphi retirees will receive a $2,000 payment in or about March 2027 covering prior years, and a future $500 payment in December 2027. Let’s be clear. This issue never should’ve taken this long to resolve. While GM makes a record $20 billion payout to Wall Street, certain Delphi retirees have had to wait years to get what they’ve been owed. Through the diligence of the UAW, and the members who raised their voices, we have made things right, and will keep fighting for every single member to get their fair share.

This September, independent student newspaper The Cornell Daily Sun broke news of a civil lawsuit brought forth by Jane Doe—a former student who dropped out following her alleged rape and assault by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. The story galvanized a nation of Jane Does, where one in four undergraduate women experience sexual assault after starting college. At Cornell University, that number recently rose to one in three. Survivors and allies took to social media, decrying how universities and legal systems have failed female student bodies for generations.
